title: Ribbon stitch
subtitle: A silk ribbon stitch that curls at the tip to make a pointed petal or leaf
excerpt: Ribbon stitch is worked by bringing the ribbon up through the fabric, laying it flat, and then piercing the needle back through the centre of the ribbon itself rather than beside it. When the ribbon is pulled through, the sides curl inward to a soft pointed tip, creating a natural petal or leaf shape in a single stitch.
sourceNotes: Silk ribbon embroidery is documented in 19th-century needlework manuals including Weldon's Practical Needlework series. Ribbon stitch technique as described in standard silk ribbon embroidery references.

content.text: Ribbon stitch produces a single petal or leaf whose tip curls gently inward without any shaping or gathering. The curl happens because the needle re-enters the fabric through the ribbon itself: as the ribbon is pulled through, its edges fold in on themselves, rolling to a point at the tip. This makes it one of the most efficient ways to build a flower from silk ribbon, since each petal is completed in one movement.

items.label: Ribbon
items.value: 4 mm or 7 mm pure silk ribbon; synthetic ribbon can be used but gives a stiffer curl

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm cotton, silk, or linen; avoid loosely woven fabric where the ribbon tip can sink through

items.label: Needle
items.value: Chenille needle size 18 for 4 mm ribbon; size 16 for 7 mm ribbon; the large eye prevents creasing the ribbon

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm embroidery hoop; keep fabric taut so the ribbon does not pull the surface

content.text: Thread the chenille needle with a 30 to 40 cm length of silk ribbon. Pierce the ribbon end about 1 cm from the tip and pull the ribbon through the eye to lock it.

Secure the ribbon tail at the back with a small knot or a few stitches in ordinary thread. Bring the needle up through the fabric at the base of the petal position, pulling the ribbon through until it lies flat on the surface.

Hold the ribbon flat against the fabric with your thumb, lying in the direction of the petal. Pierce the needle back through the centre of the ribbon at the point where you want the petal tip to be. The needle enters through the ribbon, not beside it.

Pull the ribbon gently through to the back, watching the tip form. Stop pulling as soon as the curl appears and the tip rolls inward. Do not pull tight: the looser the ribbon lies on the surface, the softer and more natural the curl. A tight pull flattens the tip and loses the characteristic shape.

Build petals and leaves by working from the centre of the flower outward. Vary the stitch length for petals of different sizes and change the angle slightly for each petal so they do not all point in the same direction.

items.symptom: The tip is flat rather than curled
items.cause: The ribbon was pulled too tight through the fabric.
items.fix: Pull only until the sides just begin to turn inward, then stop. Use a pin or the needle tip to hold the ribbon flat on the surface while you ease the ribbon through with minimum tension.

items.symptom: The ribbon twists on the surface instead of lying flat
items.cause: The ribbon twisted when it came out of the fabric or was not held flat before inserting the needle at the tip.
items.fix: After you bring the ribbon up, check it for twists. Use the needle or a spare pin to lay it flat. Then make the tip stitch.

items.symptom: The ribbon tip sinks through the fabric at the stitch point
items.cause: Ground fabric is too loosely woven for the ribbon width.
items.fix: Back the fabric with a firm interfacing or use a tightly woven ground. A fabric with a visible weave will allow the ribbon to slip through the holes rather than creating a tip on the surface.
